summary: Specifies the use of Curve25519 and Curve448 key exchange methods in the Secure Shell protocol. These elliptic curve methods let the two sides of an SSH connection agree on a shared secret.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC adds two ways for an SSH client and server to agree on a shared secret using elliptic curves. The methods are named curve25519-sha256 and curve448-sha512, and they reuse the message flow that SSH already defines for elliptic curve key exchange.

questions: how does ssh key exchange work with curve25519
subtitle: Two elliptic curve key exchange methods for SSH, built on Curve25519 and Curve448.

tldr.problem: SSH needs a way for a client and a server to agree on a shared secret. A Curve25519 key exchange was already deployed under a private name in libssh and OpenSSH but was not standardized, and Curve448 had no SSH method at all.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers the method names curve25519-sha256 and curve448-sha512. They reuse the ECDH messages and the exchange hash of RFC 5656 but compute the shared secret with the X25519 and X448 functions, using a different encoding for public values and for the final secret.
tldr.outcome: Curve25519 with SHA-256 is the preferred choice, at about 128 bits of security. Curve448 with SHA-512 is offered as a hedge at about 224 bits, in case the mathematics behind the first is ever broken.

facts.label: Hash functions
facts.value: SHA-256 for Curve25519, SHA-512 for Curve448

today: RFC 8731 is a Proposed Standard, published in February 2020. No RFC obsoletes it and no RFC updates it, so it is still the published definition of these two SSH key exchange methods.

sections.title: Elliptic Curve Key Exchange for SSH
sections.content:
Secure Shell (SSH) (RFC 4251) is a protocol for secure remote login. Its key exchange protocol (RFC 4253) supports an extensible set of methods, and RFC 5656 defines how elliptic curves are integrated into that framework. This document reuses the Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) key exchange protocol messages defined in Section 7.1 of RFC 5656. The other parts of RFC 5656, such as Elliptic Curve Menezes-Qu-Vanstone key agreement and the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm, are not considered here.

The RFC describes how to implement key exchange based on Curve25519 and Curve448 (RFC 7748) in SSH. For Curve25519 with SHA-256, the algorithm described is equivalent to the privately defined algorithm curve25519-sha256@libssh.org, which at the time of publication was implemented and widely deployed in libssh and OpenSSH. The Curve448 key exchange method is similar but uses SHA-512.
sections.plainLanguage: SSH (Secure Shell) has a pluggable set of key exchange methods. This RFC adds two built on modern elliptic curves, so that a client and a server can agree on a shared secret without either of them sending a secret over the connection.

sections.title: How the Key Exchange Runs
sections.content:
The key exchange procedure is similar to the ECDH method described in Section 4 of RFC 5656, though with a different wire encoding used for public values and for the final shared secret. Public ephemeral keys are encoded for transmission as standard SSH strings. The protocol flow, the SSH_MSG_KEX_ECDH_INIT and SSH_MSG_KEX_ECDH_REPLY messages, and the structure of the exchange hash are identical to that section of RFC 5656.

Both methods are based on Curve25519 and Curve448 scalar multiplication as described in RFC 7748, with private and public keys generated as described there. Public keys are defined as strings of 32 bytes for Curve25519 and 56 bytes for Curve448. The schemes curve25519-sha256 and curve448-sha512 perform the Diffie-Hellman protocol using the functions X25519 and X448 respectively. Implementations SHOULD compute these functions with the algorithms described in RFC 7748.

When they do, implementations MUST check whether the computed Diffie-Hellman shared secret is the all-zero value and abort if it is. Alternative implementations SHOULD abort when either the client or the server input forces the shared secret to one of a small set of values. Clients and servers MUST also abort if the length of the received public keys is not the expected length. An abort for these purposes is defined as a disconnect, SSH_MSG_DISCONNECT, of the session, and it SHOULD use the SSH_DISCONNECT_KEY_EXCHANGE_FAILED reason. No further validation is required beyond what RFC 7748 describes. The derived shared secret is 32 bytes when curve25519-sha256 is used and 56 bytes when curve448-sha512 is used, and the hash used is SHA-256 for the first method and SHA-512 for the second.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends an ephemeral public key and the server sends one back, and each side computes the same shared secret from the other's key and its own private key. Both sides must check two things before going on: that the received key is the right length, and that the shared secret is not all zeros, which would mean the other side sent a degenerate key.

sections.title: How the Shared Secret Is Encoded
sections.content:
The shared secret K is defined in RFC 4253 and RFC 5656 as an integer encoded as a multiple precision integer, an mpint. Curve25519 and Curve448 output a binary string X, which is the 32- or 56-byte point obtained by scalar multiplication of the other side's public key and the local private key scalar. The 32 or 56 bytes of X are converted into K by interpreting the octets as an unsigned fixed-length integer encoded in network byte order.

The mpint K is then encoded using the process described in Section 5 of RFC 4251, and the resulting bytes are fed as described in RFC 4253 to the key exchange method's hash function to generate the encryption keys. This step is the one that differs from RFC 5656, which uses a different conversion. The change is not intended to modify RFC 5656 generally, but applies only to the mechanism described in this document.

The order of the conversions matters. When the X25519 or X448 operations run, the integer values there are encoded into byte strings by a fixed-length unsigned little-endian conversion, as in RFC 7748. Only later, when those byte strings are passed to the ECDH function in SSH, are the bytes reinterpreted as a fixed-length unsigned big-endian integer value K. K is then encoded as a variable-length signed mpint before it is fed, along with other data, to the hash algorithm used for key generation.
sections.plainLanguage: The curve functions hand back a fixed-length byte string, but SSH expects the shared secret as a multiple precision integer. The RFC spells out the order: little-endian inside the curve math, then big-endian when it becomes the SSH secret, then the usual SSH integer encoding before it is hashed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 4251, RFC 5656 and RFC 7748 are inherited.

Curve25519 with SHA-256 provides strong security of about 128 bits, is efficient on a wide range of architectures, and has characteristics that allow for better implementation properties compared to traditional elliptic curves. Curve448 with SHA-512 provides stronger security of about 224 bits with similar implementation properties. However, it has not received the same cryptographic review as Curve25519, and it is slower, because of larger key material and a larger secure hash algorithm. It is provided as a hedge to combat unforeseen analytical advances against Curve25519 and SHA-256, due to the larger number of security bits.

The way the derived mpint binary secret string is encoded before it is hashed, which means adding or removing zero bytes for encoding, raises the potential for a side-channel attack that could determine the length of what is hashed. That would leak the most significant bit of the derived secret, or allow detection of when the most significant bytes are zero. For backwards-compatibility reasons, it was decided not to address this potential problem.

The document provides curve25519-sha256 as the preferred choice but suggests that curve448-sha512 be implemented, to provide more than 128 bits of security strength should that become a requirement.
sections.plainLanguage: Curve25519 with SHA-256 is the preferred choice, giving about 128 bits of security. Curve448 with SHA-512 gives about 224 bits and is slower, and it is offered as a backup in case the mathematics of the first is ever broken. The encoding step has a known side channel that leaks one bit of the secret; the RFC leaves it in place for compatibility.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: IANA has added curve25519-sha256 and curve448-sha512 to the "Key Exchange Method Names" registry for SSH, the registry created in Section 4.10 of RFC 4250. Those are the names that an SSH client and server use to name the method they are running.
sections.plainLanguage: The two method names have been registered so that SSH implementations can refer to them by a standard name.
